A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research, renamed from PHASEEVO to SEE. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison across substantial rewriting and relocation.

before.justification: V1 reports original prompt-optimization experiments on 35 tasks, operator studies, ablations, and a manual evaluation of generated examples.

after.justification: V2 retains original benchmark and operator results and adds model comparisons, phase-removal experiments, and few-shot controls.

M1.justification: The four phases, five operator classes, two initialization options, performance-vector Hamming distance, adaptive stopping, and greedy candidate selection remain. Appendix definitions and operator prompts confirm that SEE and its fusion terminology do not introduce a substantive procedural change.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same eight BBH tasks, three detection tasks, and 24 instruction-induction tasks. Added analyses reuse these tasks; additional LLM configurations do not change dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 Table 21 adds MoP, EASE, and ZOPO comparisons and introduces EvoPrompt and OPRO into the instruction-induction comparison. Table 4 additionally evaluates few-shot variants of OPRO and EvoPrompt. The Rhymes case study replaces InstructZero with ZOPO.

E3.justification: The reported BBH split changes from 50 training, 50 development, and 125 test examples to 125 for training/development and up to 125 for testing, without specifying the internal division. V2 replaces the two-model, eight-task BBH comparison with an eight-model, four-task study and adds token-consumption evaluation. These reported changes do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds removal of individual optimization phases in Figure 4 and random two-example augmentation of OPRO/EvoPrompt in Table 4, directly testing phase contributions and the rationale for joint optimization. It also expands analysis across LLM backends. Earlier operator studies, Hamming-distance and random-search ablations, and the synthetic-example audit are retained.

E5.justification: V1 Appendix E.2 specifies one GPT-4 BBH run; the replacement model-comparison study in v2 specifies three end-to-end runs per model with means and standard deviations. Earlier BBH means and deviations remain unchanged in v2 Table 19, so their relocation from the main table is not removal of uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial baseline, model, ablation, few-shot, and token-consumption results. Revised entries include AELP Causal Judgement, 76.47 to 77.77, and the proposed method's Logical Five best-prompt result, 82.62 in v1 Table 18 to 86.29 in v2 Table 2. Earlier BBH means remain in Table 19; revised settings and summaries prevent interpreting the main-table differences as demonstrated same-setting gains.

T1.justification: Equation 1 and the formal operator definitions retain their mathematical substance despite relocation and renumbering. The added metaheuristic overview and explanation of cohesiveness introduce no new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or mathematical objective.

C1.justification: The central joint-optimization and efficiency claims remain. V2 explicitly claims priority for dynamically producing both zero-shot and few-shot prompts and shifts the stated novelty toward strategic organization of existing operators. It also introduces headline claims of a 13.94 accuracy-point gain and 58.67% cost reduction.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations for the effects of removing phases, argues that its common parameter configuration requires little tuning, and explains exclusions from cost comparisons. It also identifies single-objective optimization as a limitation. The principal exploration/exploitation interpretation and existing online-computation limitation remain.

D1.justification: V2 newly discloses GPT-3.5-turbo's internal Azure hosting, exclusion of unsuccessful responses from accuracy calculations, and a 1% phase-transition threshold. Conversely, v1's baseline-specific notes distinguishing best-result and average-result comparisons disappear. Operator templates, pool sizes, temperatures, and tolerances are retained.

R1.justification: V2 substantially reframes the work around general metaheuristic optimization, adding Talbi and Blum–Roli references and emphasizing reuse of established operators. New Table 7 maps operators across prior methods. Adding MoP, EASE, and ZOPO, including acknowledgment of prior joint instruction/example optimization, materially expands the novelty context beyond relocating Related Work.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and methodology are extensively rewritten around SEE, cohesive optimization, and metaheuristics. V2 adds explicit contribution bullets and an Intuition subsection, moves Related Work into Appendix A, separates Limitations, and supplies an appendix roadmap.

P2.justification: V2 changes the document template and substantially reorganizes displays. It adds model, few-shot, and operator-comparison tables and a phase-ablation figure; expands the instruction-induction table; and replaces the cost scatterplot with a dual-axis API/token bar chart. Detection and uncertainty tables move into the appendix, and duplicated BBH prompt listings are removed.

improvement.justification: The new phase ablations and few-shot controls better test the central design, while additional baselines and LLM comparisons strengthen empirical support. New implementation disclosures improve transparency. These benefits are tempered by ambiguous BBH split and aggregation descriptions: higher instruction-induction win totals match selecting the better GPT-3.5/GPT-4 score and counting ties, although the individual score columns are unchanged. Overall, the evidence supports a limited net improvement.
